title: 2. Start pressing thumbs down  the negative signal the algorithm is starving for.
hook_spoken: 2. Start pressing thumbs down  the negative signal the algorithm is starving for.
transcript_30s:
2. Start pressing thumbs down  the negative signal the algorithm is starving for.

This is the single most impactful retraining action  and the one most subscribers have never taken.

Netflix has a thumbs-down button on every title. On the homepage. On the title detail page. During playback. After playback. It's everywhere. Most subscribers have never pressed it  not once, on any title, in years of usage.

Why this matters:

The algorithm learns from 2 types of signals: positive (what you watch, what you finish, what you rate up) and negative (what you skip, what you quit early, what you rate down). Most subscribers give hundreds of positive signals  they watch shows, finish episodes, add to My List. They give almost zero explicit negative signals.

Without negative signals, the algorithm has no boundaries. It knows what you'll watch. It doesn't know what you won't. So it keeps recommending the same genres  because nothing told it to stop. One true crime documentary becomes 6 rows of true crime. Not because you love true crime. Because you never told the algorithm you don't.

The retraining action:

Scroll your homepage right now. Every title you see that you'd never watch  not "maybe," not "later," genuinely "never"  press thumbs down. Korean soap opera you'd never watch? Thumbs down. Reality dating show? Thumbs down. Horror movie you'd never open? Thumbs down.

Each thumbs down tells the algorithm: "Stop showing me this type of content." It reduces that genre's weight in your recommendations. It creates space for other genres to surface. It gives the algorithm the boundary it's been missing.

He spent 5 minutes thumbs-downing 20 titles on his homepage that he'd never watch. Within 48 hours, those genres started receding. New rows appeared  categories he hadn't seen in months. The homepage opened up  because the algorithm finally knew where the edges of his taste were.

"You've been scrolling past content you don't want  for years  without telling the algorithm you don't want it. The scroll is invisible to the algorithm. The thumbs down is not. Press it. The homepage changes."

title: Agentagogy: An Instructional Framework to Address Artificial Intelligence in Learning
hook_spoken: Agentagogy: An Instructional Framework to Address Artificial Intelligence in Learning
transcript_30s:
Agentagogy: An Instructional Framework to Address Artificial Intelligence in Learning

Pedagogy, andragogy, and heutagogy remain indispensable. They help us decide who leads learning, how much structure is warranted, and when the learner should determine the path. Pedagogy orients us to guided instruction. Andragogy takes adult experience and purpose seriously. Heutagogy pushes further toward self-determined capability.

In the era of artificial intelligence and agentic agents, they are not enough.

None of those frameworks were built for learning environments in which artificial agents can plan, retrieve, write, tutor, assess, and act. The “gogy” continuum (pedagogy – andragogy – heutagogy) still assumes that the primary agents in the room are human: teacher, facilitator, or learner. Once AI can initiate, delegate, and complete cognitive work, the instructional problem changes. We are no longer only asking how to teach children, support adults, or cultivate self-determined learners. We are asking how to design teaching and learning when agency itself is shared, contested, and easily outsourced.

I recently spent time with Seth Fleischauer @LaoshiSeth and Allyson Mitchell on their “Why Distance Learning?” podcast entitled “Why Distance Learning? Episode 88 #88 This Is Online Learning's Moment to Lead - with Dr. Mark Deschaine”. I received feedback and requests for more information related to the term Agentagogy.

This post is a first public sketch, not a finished theory of that term and concept. I will continue to develop Agentagogy in future presentations and writing. The conversation that prompted these requests is here share.transistor.fm/s/ad1593… I have searched the literature, databases, and the open web for the term agentagogy. I have not found the term in use as an instructional framework. That does not make the idea automatically correct. It does mean we may be looking at a new, and potentially foundational, way to investigate AI as teaching and learning move forward.

More importantly, I believe clarification is not only important but necessary, because the adjacent term Agentivism is already in circulation.

Agentivism, as proposed by Yan and Gašević, is a learning theory. It asks how durable human capability can still grow when learners can delegate explanation, problem solving, and production to generative and agentic systems. Its concern is process: selective delegation, epistemic monitoring, reconstructive internalization, and transfer under reduced support. That work is significant: it matters, however, I do not see it as the same project.

Agentagogy is an instructional framework. It asks how we design, lead, assess, and govern learning environments in which artificial agents are participants, not merely tools. It sits in the same family as pedagogy, andragogy, and heutagogy: not “how does learning occur in the mind when AI is present,” but “how should teaching and learning be arranged when AI is present.”

This is not a syllogism.
Agent + -agogy ≠ a clever rename of Agentivism.

The distinction matters for practice, and research investigations into that practice. A learning theory can explain why completed work may not equal learned capability. An instructional framework must answer different questions: When should an agent tutor, collaborate, or step back? What remains of the teacher’s responsibility? How do we preserve learner judgment when fluency is cheap? What counts as evidence of learning when performance can be assembled by a system? How do curriculum, assessment, ethics, and leadership change when the learning environment includes nonhuman actors?

If we collapse those questions into a theory of human–AI cognition, we will keep describing the problem while leaving instructors, programs, and institutions without a design language. If we treat Agentagogy as wordplay, we will miss why the older “gogies” strain under agentic systems: they allocate agency among humans. They do not tell us how to teach when agency can be automated.

Agentagogy, as I am developing it, is an attempt to not only name that instructional gap, but begin filling it. It does not replace pedagogy, andragogy, or heutagogy. It asks what must be added when artificial intelligence is no longer an accessory to the learning environment but a condition of it.

This is the introduction to the concept. The important work and heavy lifting come next. I have several projects in various stages of authorship in hopes to begin important conversations around the integration of artificial intelligence into learning and teaching environs.

Acknowledgement of AI statement: In true agentagogical form, Super Grok was utilized to assist with this post.

Builders start with open-source templates, write in familiar languages, and use the AI coding tools they already know.

Instead of deploying another smart contract onto someone else’s blockspace, the product launches as a Nested Chain: an application-specific chain with its own logic, economics, and upgrade path.

Canopy’s most interesting potential moat, however, may be its open-source flywheel. Every public application could expand a library of working examples for future coding agents.

➥ Final Thesis

More apps → smarter agents → shorter build cycles → even more apps and CNPY adoption.

That’s the core Canopy thesis, and it’s what ends up expressed in CNPY.

Not a ghost chain hoping developers show up someday, but an AI-first assembly line where the concept, the app, the chain, the security, and the token launch ship in one unbroken pipeline.

transcript_30s:
"Alone In the Wilderness" In 1968 at the age of 51, Richard “Dick” Proenneke made a decision that would completely change the rest of his life. After years working as a diesel mechanic, he abandoned his job and the comforts of modern society and traveled to the isolated Twin Lakes region of Alaska. Instead of simply camping there, Proenneke intended to build a permanent home with his own hands.

Using little more than the resources available around him, he began constructing a log cabin from scratch. He felled trees for the walls, collected gravel from the bed of a nearby lake to create a solid foundation and hauled heavy stones from the surrounding wilderness to build the fireplace. Everything had to be done manually, with no modern construction crew coming to help him.

Once the cabin was finished, Proenneke settled into an extraordinary life of isolation. For roughly three decades, he lived almost completely alone in the Alaskan wilderness, relying mainly on hunting, fishing and gathering wild food to survive. He remained there until he was 83, when age finally convinced him to leave. He moved to California and spent his final years living with his brother.

What makes Proenneke's story even more remarkable is that he documented much of his experience himself. Using an 8mm camera, he filmed the construction of his cabin, the surrounding wilderness and the everyday challenges of living completely alone. After his death in 2003, only four years after he had left Alaska, those recordings were assembled into the documentary Alone in the Wilderness, allowing others to see how he had lived.

Proenneke also made sure that his home would survive after him. He left the cabin to the National Park Service, which preserved it as part of America's historical heritage. Today, the remote cabin remains a popular attraction for visitors and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, turning the home of an Alaskan hermit into a lasting piece of history.

Korean Air signed the definitive contracts in Seoul for 103 Boeing jets, 50 of them 737-10s, the fleet it wants once it has absorbed Asiana. Thirteen months ago this was a memorandum announced in Washington as a $50 billion purchase. It closed at $44.8 billion.

The airplanes did not move. They were $36.2 billion in the August 2025 memorandum and they are $36.2 billion today, to the dollar. What changed is the piece bolted on next to them: the spare engines and the GE Aerospace maintenance contract went from about $13.7 billion over 20 years to $8.6 billion over 15, on the same 28 aircraft. transcript_30s:
Building a million dollar agency from Sri Lanka. Nobody saw that coming. Not even me.

It started simple. I knew design. Thimasha knew design. We had two laptops and a problem we genuinely wanted to solve. Founders were spending a fortune on creative and getting chaos in return. We figured we could fix that.

So we built an offer around it and started knocking on doors.

For three months nothing happened.

Cold outreach. Ads. Platforms. Product Hunt. Every single thing we could think of. Zero clients. Zero revenue. Just two people in a room refusing to quit.

Then one night I was dialing leads at midnight and a lady picked up. I figured out she was Sri Lankan. Asked her. She laughed and said yes. We jumped on a call.

That was Upeka from Diana, YC W24. Our first client. She did not just give us the work. She introduced us to a world we did not know existed. The SF startup ecosystem. YC founders. Everything Zyner is today traces back to that one phone call.

From there we learned everything the hard way.

Lost clients. Delivered work that was not good enough and had to own it. Figured out that great design with bad project management is useless. That great project management with no creative direction is equally useless. That all of it means nothing if the client does not feel like they are being taken care of.

We kept going anyway.

Team went from 5 to 80. Clients went from 1 to 320+. Revenue crossed $1M ARR.

Here is what actually made the difference.

We hired slowly. Every single person trained properly before touching a client file. No shortcuts on that. Ever.

We built SOPs before we needed them. Every scenario documented. Everyone knows exactly what to do when things go wrong. And things always go wrong at some point.

We stayed close to clients. I still reply on every Slack thread personally. Not because I have to. Because I want to. The relationship matters as much as the work.

We charged what the work was worth. The moment we stopped being scared about pricing everything changed. Better clients. Better projects. Better outcomes.

And we never stopped showing up online. Posts. Case studies. Sharing the story. Inbound does not happen in a week. It happens after months of consistency that most people give up on too early.

That is the whole thing honestly.

No secret. No shortcut. Just showing up every single day and refusing to quit on something worth building.

If you are building a service business right now and wondering if it is possible. It is. I promise you it is.

I picked up somebody in the area, and we were driving on the highway. We looked to the side of us and we noticed orange flames coming from under a car, and she was still driving. I just knew I couldn't keep going and not stop. I had to do something. She started to pull over. So I pulled over, and my passenger told me there was two kids in the car too. So I jump out, I run back there, and we got the mother and kids out of the car safely. I called the fire department. By the time they got there, the whole engine was engulfed. The hood was burned away. - It's burning! - Stay back. - What was going through my mind when I saw that is I can't let it go, I cannot drive away and not know that they're okay, 'cause what if something happened when I could have done something? This is what I do. I take pride in my work, and I take that seriously that I'm getting people where they need to go safely. I think we all have to... help each other. I think it is our responsibility to help each other out. That's the essence of community. It's just being there for each other. [uplifting music]

title: Galaxy Day 1 in two minutes.
hook_spoken: Galaxy Day 1 in two minutes.
transcript_30s:
Galaxy Day 1 in two minutes.

What Grok Bot is: named, persistent AI teammates. Each has one job, its own memory, and shares one cloud computer per account with a browser, files, and your logins. You message them like colleagues. They run routines while you're away. Anything in production goes to a Cursor Cloud Agent in an isolated VM; the bot manages the agent and reads back the PR.

What a bot is made of: Instructions, Memories, Skills, Routines, Integrations. Publish one as a template and anyone can import it.

What each session said:

Engineers: nightly repo audits, auto-fix on any CI alert, a reviewer bot on every PR, a routine that checks a Cloud Agent every five minutes and interrupts it if it drifts. Verification first: without a verification skill every PR ends with "click around and check it out."

PMs: an attention list synthesized from Slack, email, and meetings. One PM runs eleven bots grouped into pods. Highest-leverage onboarding instruction: "read my past Slack and develop a style guide."

Founders: a close bot that handles customers end to end, a stalk bot that signs up for competitors' products, a proto bot that turns feedback into PRs. Browser use is the expensive primitive; have the bot learn the API from network requests and call it directly next time.

The team also started a company on stream. GitHub org "Ship by Thursday," a pop-up restaurant platform (maybe?... it sounded like a pivot was going to happen when they signed off yesterday). Goal is to be live within 72 hours.

One thing I learned by playing around: importing a template isn't a file copy. The new bot reads the template and rebuilds itself, action by action. I imported @poteto 's dr eggbot and re-exported it. Skills survive only if self-contained. Net: Good templates carry their own setup procedure in memory.

The challenge: publish a bot template, share how it fits your work, tag @grok and @bot . Prize is a Starship launch seat for you and a guest!

title: Higher fuel prices squeeze $UBER $GRAB mainly through its drivers, who pay for gas themselves as independent contractors. The companies does not au…
hook_spoken: Higher fuel prices squeeze $UBER $GRAB mainly through its drivers, who pay for gas themselves as independent contractors. The companies does not automatically reimburse fuel, so costs hit driver earnings first and then ripple through supply, pricing, and trip volume.
transcript_30s:
Higher fuel prices squeeze $UBER $GRAB mainly through its drivers, who pay for gas themselves as independent contractors. The companies does not automatically reimburse fuel, so costs hit driver earnings first and then ripple through supply, pricing, and trip volume.

Fuel is a large share of operating costs. When prices rise sharply, net pay falls unless drivers work longer hours or become more selective.

Fewer available drivers can tighten supply. Uber’s marketplace then uses dynamic pricing (including surge) to rebalance, so riders may see higher fares or longer waits in busy periods.

In some countries, Uber has added a temporary extra fee on trips (and sometimes Uber Eats) that goes 100% to the driver.

However, demand falls when prices rise (studies have found roughly a 0.4% drop in trips for every 1% rise in fuel prices). Competition from Lyft, taxis, public transit, or simply staying home.

Lastly, $GRAB operates in some of the most volatile region in the world. When drivers/delivery person gets paycut due to surge in fuel, and if commuters/consumers felt price raises too quickly, political unrest might happen.

THIS IS GRAPH ENGINEERING, the layer that decides how much thinking each step of a job is allowed to buy, and it runs inside the plan you already pay for:

1. click the model name next to the send button, open Effort, set Low. in ChatGPT the same menu is called reasoning level. run a normal day like that

2. when one step decides the outcome, raise it for that message only and drop it back after: Fable 5.1 keeps everything it already read, so the switch costs nothing

3. before the next big job open Settings → Usage, note the number, run the job, look again

turns out the setting decides the bill, and both companies picked it for you

on Low, Fable 5.1 looks things up less and answers from memory more, so anything about this week goes back to High

almost five answers from the best model on earth for the price of one, on the plan you already have

hook_spoken: I posted before about my "epiphany" with the Cummins diesel. It's hard to believe that a 1995 12 valve blew the doors off my worked 1996 Impala SS.
transcript_30s:
I posted before about my "epiphany" with the Cummins diesel. It's hard to believe that a 1995 12 valve blew the doors off my worked 1996 Impala SS.

The Cat 3208 lost to Cummins and Caterpillar inline engines partly because its non-removable liners made rebuilds harder. The GMC Toro-Flow lost because the service network could not support its toroidal prechamber. The GMC 270 died because GM consolidated truck engines and shared parts won. Every commercial engine story on this page ends the same way: the winner is not the engine with the best specification sheet, it is the engine that the parts counter and the service bay can support.

Cummins just made that the entire product strategy.
The L9 and the X12 are both discontinued. In their place is the X10, a 10-liter inline-six that covers both markets from a single architecture. Medium-duty calibrations run 320 to 380 horsepower and 1,000 to 1,250 lb-ft. Heavy-duty calibrations run 350 to 450 horsepower and 1,350 to 1,650 lb-ft. Same block, same heads, same rotating assembly. The range is covered through calibration, turbocharger sizing, and aftertreatment configuration rather than through separate engine families.

It slots between the B6.7, which is the 6.7-liter descendant of the 5.9 that saved Dodge's truck division in 1989, and the X15, which is the Class 8 long-haul engine in Peterbilts and Kenworths. The L9 handled the bottom of that gap and the X12 handled the top. One engine now handles both.

For a fleet running 200 trucks across mixed duty cycles, that consolidation is worth more than any horsepower figure. Two engine families means two parts inventories, two sets of filters and gaskets and injectors, two training curricula for technicians, two service manuals, and two supply chains that can each fail independently. One family cuts all of it in half. That is the number that moves a purchase order.

The emissions work is where the engineering lives. Cummins claims 75 percent lower NOx than required at launch, meeting the EPA's 2027 regulations a year early. A belt-driven 48-volt alternator replaces the traditional 12-volt system, which generates electrical power more efficiently and allows electric-assist accessories that pull less parasitic load off the crankshaft. An aftertreatment heater gets the catalyst to operating temperature faster, because a cold catalyst does nothing and most NOx violations happen in the first minutes after startup. Compatibility with B20 biodiesel and renewable diesel.

Then Acumen, which is the part that has no precedent anywhere on this page. Over-the-air software updates. Predictive maintenance flagging. Real-time monitoring through a fleet platform. A calibration change can be pushed to every engine in a fleet from a desk without a single truck visiting a shop. A fuel economy improvement or an emissions update reaches 200 trucks simultaneously.

Compare that to every engine covered. The Slant Six needed a timing light and a feeler gauge. The Ford 300 required oil changes and a valve adjustment. The 12-valve Cummins earned its cult following specifically because it had no electronics to fail, with a mechanical P7100 injection pump that a mechanic could service in a field. The X10 is the opposite philosophy taken to its conclusion: the engine's behavior is software, and software arrives over the air.

Whether that is an improvement depends entirely on whom you ask. A fleet manager gets calibration updates without downtime. An owner-operator gets an engine whose behavior can change without him touching it. The 12-valve crowd will tell you which of those they prefer and they will not be quiet about it.

The X10 will not appear in a pickup. It will not appear in a race. It will appear in the truck that delivers packages to your street, the bus that carries children, and the chassis that plows the road in February. The X10 will not appear in a pickup. It will not appear in a race. It will appear in the truck that delivers packages to your street, the bus that carries children, and the chassis that plows the road in February. The engines that matter most have always been the ones nobody thinks about.

title: I’m a startup founder in Miami who also drives Uber nights and weekends to make ends meet. @Uber , I want the platform to succeed. But I don’t thin…
hook_spoken: I’m a startup founder in Miami who also drives Uber nights and weekends to make ends meet. @Uber , I want the platform to succeed. But I don’t think we’re measuring driver economics correctly.
transcript_30s:
I’m a startup founder in Miami who also drives Uber nights and weekends to make ends meet. @Uber , I want the platform to succeed. But I don’t think we’re measuring driver economics correctly.

I reviewed 7 recent UberX rides from my own account. Excluding tips and toll reimbursements:

57.03 passenger-trip miles
2 hours 4 minutes with riders
$62.28 in driver earnings before vehicle expenses

If you look only at pickup-to-drop-off time, that appears to be about $30/hour gross.

But that’s not a driver’s working clock.

Our time starts when we accept the ride and begin driving to the passenger.

If the drive to those 7 pickups averaged just 10 minutes each, my active time is already at least 3 hours 14 minutes, and the same $62.28 becomes about $19.26/hour gross.

And that’s before counting additional pickup waiting.

It’s also before energy, depreciation, tires, maintenance, cleaning and insurance.

And it still excludes time online between rides and repositioning after a drop-off.

Uber itself has used a definition of “active time” that includes driving to pickup, waiting and completing the trip.

There’s another problem: paid wait time generally doesn’t begin until we reach the designated pickup point and the rider’s grace period expires.

In Miami, real life isn’t always that clean.

At a gated community, I can be sitting at the gate waiting for access while the app doesn’t consider me at the pickup.

At an event, reaching a passenger can take 20–30+ minutes.

If traffic or police make me circle while the rider is still inside, I’m still committing my time and vehicle to that ride, but the paid-wait clock may not reflect it.

My receipt shows paid waiting at $0.19/minute, or $11.40/hour, once that clock is actually running.

Here’s another benchmark that caught my attention:

NYC’s 2026 minimum Uber/Lyft driver-pay formula is $1.283/mile + $0.681/minute.

Apply that formula to the same 57.03 passenger miles and 124 passenger minutes and the minimum comes to about $157.61.

My actual earnings on those Miami rides were $62.28.

NYC is a different market and more expensive overall. I’m not saying Miami should copy NYC.

But a ~2.5x difference is large enough to ask whether Miami’s driver economics are calibrated correctly.

And this matters competitively.

Driver-first alternatives are targeting exactly this pain point. Empower launched in Miami this year with a model that lets drivers set their own rates and keep the fare while paying the platform separately. Epic Rides is local and signing hundreds of drivers per week.

I’m already seeing riders and drivers experiment with alternatives because cancellations, long pickup times and difficulty getting rides accepted hurt both sides.

Uber has an enormous liquidity advantage today.

But if better economics start pulling driver supply elsewhere, the consequences show up as longer ETAs and more cancellations. Eventually riders follow the supply.

That’s how a driver-economics problem can become a market-share problem.

I’m not arguing Uber should simply take less margin.

I’m not arguing riders should simply pay dramatically more.

I’m arguing that better driver economics can also mean more reliable supply, shorter pickups, fewer cancellations, less deadhead mileage and potentially less money required to incentivize supply.

That can be good for riders, drivers AND shareholders.

This is a small sample from my own driving, not a claim that 7 rides represent all of Miami.

I’m using it to illustrate what I think is a measurement problem. @Uber : I’d genuinely like to see Miami driver economics published using total active time, actual pickup time, realistic vehicle costs and tips separated.

That’s the number that matters.

I’m not someone who comes with a problem without a solution.

I put what I’d test in the next post.

transcript_30s:
JULIEN, C’EST MOI ! (What complete betrayal of Stendhal’s legacy with this latest celebration of a romanticism that his masterful Rouge et le Noir novel had so brilliantly taken apart?)

“I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little loves little.”

Jesus (Luke 7:47)

“The lady doth protest too much, methinks.”

Shakespeare (Hamlet, III, 2)

“You made us come all this way to show us what: a French triangle?”

Eglinton (Ulysses, James Joyce, 1922)

“If we knew how to analyze our loves better, we would often see that women please us only because of the counterweight of the men we have to dispute them with (…) once that counterweight is removed, the woman’s charm falls away. We have an example in the man who, feeling his taste for the woman he loves weakening, spontaneously applies the rules he has worked out, and, to make sure he does not stop loving her, places her in a dangerous milieu where he must protect her every day.”

Proust (The Prisoner, 1923)

A person who knew Mlle Amélie Bosquet, Flaubert’s correspondent, very intimately, recently told me that when Mlle Bosquet asked the novelist where he had drawn the character of Mme Bovary from, he answered very clearly, and repeated several times: “Mme Bovary, c’est moi! — According to me.”

René Descharmes (1909)

“As for love, it has been the great subject of reflection of my whole life. (…) the heart I was studying was my own. How many times, in my best moments, have I felt the cold of the scalpel entering my flesh! Bovary (…) will be, in this respect, the sum of my psychological knowledge and will have original value only on that side.”

Gustave Flaubert (letter to Louise Colet, 3 July 1852)

“I have always sinned in that respect; I have always put myself into everything I have done. In the place of Saint Anthony, for example, it is I who am there.”

Gustave Flaubert (letter to Louise Colet, 5–6 July 1852)

“Bovary was for me a matter of principle, a theme. Everything I love is not in it.”

Gustave Flaubert (letter to Edma Roger des Genettes, 30 October 1856)

“Speaking alone with myself, two steps from death, I am still a hypocrite… O nineteenth century!”

Julien (The Red and the Black, Stendhal, 1830)

“No, my reader, I was not a soldier at Wagram in 1809. You must know that forty-five years before you it was fashionable to have been a soldier under Napoleon. (…) The fact is that I was a quartermaster-sergeant and second lieutenant in the 6th Dragoons when that regiment arrived in Italy, May 1800 I believe, and that I resigned at the time of the little peace of 1803. (…) I did not become a colonel, as I would have with the powerful protection of my cousin Count Daru, but I was, I believe, much happier. I soon no longer thought of studying M. de Turenne and imitating him; that idea had been my fixed goal during the three years I was a dragoon. Sometimes it was combated by another: to write comedies like Molière and live with an actress.”

Stendhal (The Life of Henry Brulard, 1890)

“The habitual state of my life has been that of an unhappy lover, loving music and painting (…) I see that reverie is what I have preferred to everything, even to passing for a man of wit.”

Stendhal (1890)

“I see today that a quality common to all my friends was naturalness or the absence of hypocrisy. Mme Vignon and my aunt Séraphie had given me, for this first condition of success in present-day society, a horror that has done me much harm and that goes as far as physical disgust. Prolonged society with a hypocrite gives me the beginning of nausea.”

Stendhal (The Life of Henry Brulard, 1890)

“In the morning, when he arrived at the prison of Besançon, they were kind enough to lodge him on the upper floor of a Gothic keep. He judged the architecture to be from the beginning of the fourteenth century; he admired its grace and piquant lightness. Through a narrow interval between two walls beyond a deep courtyard, he had a superb glimpse of the view. (…) His prison was situated at the top of the citadel’s keep; the view stretched far over the magnificent plains of Franche-Comté.”

Stendhal (The Red and the Black, 1830)

“I cannot speak to you like that in a minute of the greatest, but you would see in Stendhal a certain feeling of altitude linked to the spiritual life, the high place where Julien Sorel is a prisoner, the tower at the top of which Fabrice is confined, the steeple where Abbé Blanès occupies himself with astrology and from which Fabrice casts such a beautiful glance.”

Marcel Proust (The Prisoner, 1923)

“Exclusive taste for the sensations of the soul, revival of the past, detachment from ambitions and boredom with intrigue, either near death (Julien in prison: no more ambition. Love for Mme de Rênal, for nature, for reverie), or as a result of the detachment caused by love (Fabrice in prison, but here the prison does not mean death, but love for Clélia). This elevation of the soul linked to physical elevation in height (Julien’s prison very high, hence a beautiful view, Fabrice’s prison very high, hence a beautiful view).”

Proust (sheets, notes and preparatory drafts)

“Stendhal, the enemy of hypocrites, (…) treats himself as a hypocrite in the conclusion of The Red and the Black. (…) The novelist recognizes himself as guilty of the sin of which he accuses his mediator. The curse that Oedipus launched against the Others falls back on his own head. It is this curse that Flaubert’s famous cry expresses: ‘Mme Bovary, c’est moi!’ Mme Bovary was first conceived as that contemptible Other whom Flaubert had sworn to settle accounts with. Mme Bovary is first Flaubert’s enemy as Julien Sorel is Stendhal’s enemy (…). But the novel’s hero, without ever ceasing to be the Other, gradually joins the novelist in the course of creation. When Flaubert cries ‘Mme Bovary, c’est moi,’ he does not mean that Mme Bovary is henceforth one of those flattering doubles with which romantic writers love to surround themselves. He means that the Self and the Other become one in the novelistic miracle. Great novelistic creations are always the fruit of a fascination that has been overcome. (…) The task is all the more difficult because the novelist himself sometimes tries to mislead us. Stendhal attributes Julien Sorel’s ‘German mysticism’ to an overly damp dungeon. The conclusion of The Red and the Black nevertheless remains a meditation on Christian themes and symbols. The novelist reaffirms his skepticism there, but the themes and symbols are no less present for being wrapped in negations.”

René Girard (1968)

“I find the end of the series phenomenal. The emotion is incredible, I had goosebumps! I was apprehensive about shooting that scene, of course. Julien says strong, surprising things… I didn’t know whether the character should crack or not. I discussed it with Gaël (…) So he doesn’t crack, even at that moment. What was hard was staying at that precise moment in the posture and coldness in which the character finds himself throughout the story, while something chilling is unfolding.”

Victor Belmondo

“I find what we did very fresh. It’s Gossip Girl in costumes. Like Dan Humphrey, Julien Sorel is a brilliant outsider trying to break into the privileged world. I would really like young people not to be afraid and to watch the series, because despite the period sets and costumes, I am convinced they can completely identify with our characters.”

Camille Razat

Promised to Mathilde de La Mole (Camille Razat), who is expecting his child, Julien finally touches his dream. But a letter from Louise de Rênal (Virginie Ledoyen) comes to annihilate his hopes of marriage and social ascent. Caught up by his choices, he sees the nets of a world he thought he had conquered close around him. As the country tips and the established order cracks, he finds himself facing his tragic and irrevocable destiny.

Allociné

The mini-series Le Rouge et le Noir concludes with an intense finale carried by Victor Belmondo and Camille Razat (…) Since its first broadcast, the work has fascinated with its narrative daring and the accuracy of its performances. While the broadcast of the second and final part captivated viewers this Monday, 7 September from 9:10 p.m., the public held its breath before the tragic fate of Julien Sorel, destined for a radiant future before seeing his hopes shattered. At Canneséries 2026, the two leading actors returned for AlloCiné to talk about this unique experience, particularly marked by the shooting of final scenes as trying as they were unforgettable. The tension was palpable in the last episode, where Julien Sorel hopes to rise into high society, supported by the love of Mathilde who is expecting their child. But everything collapses with the intervention of Louise de Rênal, whose letter wrecks his hopes of marriage and social ascent.

Oh My Mag

"Absolute horror. No need to list the errors, the buffooneries and the absurdities; they jump out at anyone who knows the work even a little. But just a reminder: Julien Sorel is very young, he is slim, frail, not very tall, at 19, and from a distance he looks like a young girl (hence Mme de Rênal’s mistake at the beginning!). Do you think Belmondo’s son has that physique, with his hairy chest?!?! As for Mme de Rênal, she is 29…. Do you think the fifty-year-old who plays her here is well chosen? One thinks one is dreaming! It’s sad, for a work so important in French culture"…

Yves Grava 

I propose (…) to re-examine the case of Stendhal’s Le Rouge et le Noir (…) on the occasion of the broadcast on France Télévisions of a four-episode series that adapts the novel: an object I find half-successful, but is the source material really that good? – Le Rouge et le Noir: it is the story of a young man from an artisan family in the Franche-Comté of 1828. Of weak constitution and vaguely intellectual, he is destined for the priesthood when his father sends him to be tutor to the children of the mayor of Verrières, a certain Monsieur de Rênal. Frustrated by nature, fiery only when he feels he has the means, Julien quickly tries to seduce the mistress of the house, who resists weakly, then no longer at all, until the rumor of her infidelity circulates and Julien is forced to leave the village. He then goes to Besançon, where he enters the seminary, then to Paris, where he quickly seduces a young noblewoman, Mathilde de La Mole, whose hand he almost obtains, until Madame de Rênal, jealous, denounces him throughout the region as a hypocrite and seducer. Julien, mad with rage, shoots his former mistress, appears before a court, out of pride does not defend himself, and dies on the guillotine. (…) what strikes me on rereading is how dry Le Rouge et le Noir is, with a strange rhythm that dwells on some episodes and skips others with the same casualness. (…) Besides the historical didacticism, the series seems to yield to several French passions: developing a secondary servant character to draw a love triangle; freezing Julien Sorel in the posture of a domestic when in the novel he is from the start in a kind of intermediate social space; correcting the misogyny of the text, or believing it does so by making Madame de Rênal a passionate and self-assured woman when Stendhal makes her a child-woman full of inconsistencies. Above all, the series transforms the heroes into romantic characters, drowning the carnal encounters in music, showing Julien contemplating the Jura like Caspar David Friedrich’s Wanderer with Schubert on the soundtrack, and thus erasing Stendhal’s very particular irony. An irony that constantly degrades the characters, and Julien in particular: choleric rather than wounded, despising the aristocracy less from opinion than from frustration, who works less for the interests of his class than for his own fate alone, and for whom idealism, very moderate, is a form of opportunism. On rereading Le Rouge et le Noir, I find the characters quite unsympathetic and this representation of the world particularly cruel, at times bordering on a superior cynicism that is not even supported by the rigor of the narrative, and finally I understand the series’ obvious intention to lift them out of mediocrity. And then, as far as irony is concerned, it is said, I prefer Flaubert.

Lucile Commeaux (France Culture, 2026) jcdurbant.wordpress.com/2026…

NAF RECEIVES FIVE NEW HELICOPTERS AS FG ACCELERATES AIRPOWER MODERNISATION

The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) has taken delivery of five new helicopters as the Federal Government accelerates efforts to modernise Nigeria’s airpower capabilities and strengthen the Armed Forces’ capacity to respond effectively to contemporary security challenges. The platforms comprise three AW-109 Trekker B helicopters manufactured by Leonardo Helicopters of Italy and two H-125 helicopters manufactured by Airbus Helicopters. The three AW-109s, which form part of 10 recently acquired by the Federal Government, were received in Lagos on 15 September 2026, with the remaining seven expected to be delivered before the end of 2026. The two H-125s had been delivered earlier.

Speaking on the development, the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, described the acquisition as “another significant milestone in the Federal Government’s sustained investment in the modernisation and re-equipment of the NAF”, noting that the new platforms would increase asset availability and enhance the Service’s responsiveness across multiple theatres. “The arrival of these five helicopters provides greater flexibility in the employment of airpower in support of ground troops in ongoing operations,” he stated.

The CAS expressed profound appreciation to the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, for his sustained confidence in and commitment to the NAF. “On behalf of the officers, airmen and airwomen of the Nigerian Air Force, I express our profound appreciation to Mr President for his sustained support for the transformation and modernisation of the Service. His commitment is enabling us to progressively build the capabilities required to meet our operational responsibilities and confront the nation’s evolving security challenges,” he said.

Air Marshal Aneke noted that the three AW-109 Trekker B helicopters would enhance NAF capabilities in intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, close air support, armed escort, combat search and rescue, as well as other joint operations in support of surface forces. He added that the two H-125 helicopters would provide versatile and responsive light helicopter support for a range of operational requirements, collectively expanding the Service’s flexibility and capacity to respond to evolving operational demands.

Following their arrival, the new platforms are undergoing post-delivery assembly ahead of their induction and operationalisation, including the necessary technical and crew-readiness processes. The CAS stressed that the NAF’s responsibility is to ensure that the investment translates into tangible operational effects. “We will continue to prioritise effective employment, maintenance and logistics sustainment so that every aircraft delivered adds measurable value to ongoing operations and the protection of the lives and property of Nigerians,” he stated. He added that the increased rotary-wing capacity would strengthen support to joint forces in countering terrorism, kidnapping and banditry, while improving the speed, reach and effectiveness of air support to forces on the ground.

The delivery of the five helicopters marks another major milestone in the Federal Government’s drive to modernise Nigeria’s airpower and strengthen the operational capabilities of the Armed Forces. Beyond expanding the NAF fleet, the new platforms are expected to enhance operational flexibility, responsiveness and sustainability, providing additional capacity to deliver decisive airpower effects in support of joint operations, protect communities and contribute to a safer and more secure Nigeria.

The headline is not “a robot installs solar.”

The real story: power deployment is becoming a manufacturing problem.

Planted says it completed field construction on a 28 MW behind-the-meter project in under 3 months, and is targeting 100 MW deployed in 2026 after more than 10 MW in 2025.

If this model works at scale, the winners won’t just be robotics companies.

They’ll include:

- Project-finance lenders
- Robot maintenance and fleet-operations providers
- Battery, spares, and remote-monitoring suppliers
- EPC and grid-interconnection partners
- Insurers learning to underwrite robotic construction
- Data-center developers buying “powered land”

The robot is only the visible layer.

The economic shift is that electricity capacity could become a manufactured output—not a one-off construction project.

What to watch: can robot-built power projects become reliably financeable at hundreds-of-megawatts scale?

title: Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Eric Goode (documentary filmmaker)
hook_spoken: Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Eric Goode (documentary filmmaker)
transcript_30s:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Eric Goode (documentary filmmaker)

Overview
Eric Goode is a documentary filmmaker whose work on Tiger King, Chimp Crazy, and Monsters of God grew out of a life that has moved through nightlife, hotels, and conservation before turning to film. The throughline is a long-running obsession with animals, especially reptiles and turtles, and an ability to gain access to morally compromised people. His story is less a clean biography than a set of hard-won pivots: clubs taught him to build worlds and networks, hotels gave him resources, conservation gave him purpose, and documentaries gave him a way to chase both truth and dopamine. The result is an argument about extinction, complicity, advocacy, and the uncomfortable empathy required to document people who harm animals.

Key Themes
- Goode rejects neat biographical framing and treats internet summaries as unreliable; his life resists a single arc.
- His parents shaped two competing inheritances: a gay artist father he understood late, and a naturalist mother who taught him to love creatures.
- A Northern California childhood saturated with EST, Esalen, and communes left him over-indoctrinated rather than converted.
- Clubs like Area were creative labs and social cross-pollinators, but rarely lucrative; hotels were the businesses that funded later interests.
- His transition to conservation came from a private, long-held reptile obsession that he kept largely closeted in New York.
- Tiger King's legacy includes real policy change, but effective advocacy requires reaching the unconverted rather than preaching to the already convinced.
- Monsters of God argues that complicity is shared and that unintended consequences of well-meaning laws are central to wildlife crime.
- Animal obsession functions like addiction: it fills a void, supplies self-worth, and can ruin lives.
- Access is the core documentary challenge; danger arrives when subjects feel used or affected by the consequences of being filmed.

Detailed Summary
Eric Goode is presented as someone who has lived what the host calls 25 lives, and he resists the tidy version. He dismisses internet and Wikipedia details as unreliable, joking that peer review is inaccurate too. Born in Rhode Island and later in Georgia, he moved around young, passed through Westchester, New York, and spent formative and high school years in Marin County and Sonoma County. He moved to New York in 1977 and stayed for more than 40 years.

His family was five kids, dysfunctional, and frequently fighting. His father was an artist, a professor, and gay, moving often because he could not hold jobs well. His mother was a naturalist and conservationist, and the household filled with tropical fish, rats, snakes, lizards, dogs, and cats. Goode says he learned a love of creatures from her. The family is from Kerala, India, and Padman is a shortened version of a longer surname changed by his grandfather. He has only been to India once, at age five, though he thought it was age four until his mother corrected him.

The Northern California environment was saturated with EST, Esalen, communes, and figures like Joseph Campbell. Esalen used the family ranch every summer. Goode attended EST around age 15 or 16, where he was told to get on the floor and relive his birth, an experience he describes as chaotic and confusing. He says he rejected the whole milieu because he was over-indoctrinated. He identifies as dyslexic and possibly ADHD, was bad in school, and got kicked out of multiple schools, including his father's alternative high school, the School of Arts and Sciences, for cheating on a geometry test. He attended two art schools, one in San Francisco and Parsons, and says he was kicked out again after the foundation year.

New York nightlife became his real education. He attributes early success to clubs functioning as labs for ideas and cross-pollination, at a time before cell phones, internet, or social media. Area opened in 1983, after Studio 54's owners went to prison, and he says they helped promote Area after getting out. It ran a little less than four years; he notes a three-year run in New York nightlife is like dog years, because clubs are ephemeral. Collaborations included Andy Warhol, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Keith Haring. He and Basquiat used to do their birthday parties together. He met Basquiat, Haring, and others in the late '70s through the nightclub scene. Drugs then were cocaine, quaaludes, heroin, and alcohol; meth was not an urban drug in the way it is today. He says he was a late bloomer with addiction and had no money early on, so drug use was opportunistic while he focused on surviving. Andy Warhol once asked on Andy Warhol TV what he would do with his money, and Goode said he would get cool tortoises.

He spent a lot of time on the Bowery and started the Maritime. A guest recounts staying at the Maritime Hotel in summer 2005 while working on Baby Mama, eating at Laeta/Loetga, and having a life-affirming moment there. That guest called the hotel operator every morning for coffee and learned she worked in the basement, was a writer for Vice, had a book called Dear Diary, and admired Amy Poehler. The guest brought the book to the Baby Mama set and gave it to Amy Poehler, leading to the writer later writing on Girls and creating her own Netflix show. The operator was Leslie Orphan. Zoe Cassavetes, John Cassavetes's daughter, also worked in the hotel basement for a while.

Hotel ownership surfaced hidden operational realities: deaths by suicide in rooms, housekeeping not entering affected rooms until they are blessed or cleansed, usually by a priest, and reputational effects such as haunted-hotel rumors. At the Maritime, guests told ghost stories, including one woman who said a ghost had sex with her. Goode's grandparents owned the Colonial Motor Inn on the border of Indiana and Michigan, where his grandmother repeatedly found dead bodies over her tenure. The Bowery Hotel keys are large brass fobs with tassels and the room number carved into the brass. The host took a key fob from room 1111 after being told the keys are not for sale but can be charged if taken. Goode also owns Hotel El Roblar in Ojai, which uses brass cowboy hats on the farm that guests take, leading to charges. He owns a tortoise hotel and conservancy in Ojai and says he is better at tortoise hospitality than human hospitality. Hotels were great businesses that afforded resources for other ventures; clubs were fun in youth and not really profitable. He describes a pattern of figuring something out, succeeding, then moving on rather than repeating the same business indefinitely.

Conservation came from a long-held private interest in reptiles and turtles, which he kept largely closeted in New York. He had reptiles and tortoises in his apartment despite social friction. In the early 1980s he incorporated animals into club themes, including a great horned owl, bats, and a 15-foot python that escaped under floorboards and was found years later as a skeleton. He says he slept with a tegu, a large black-and-white South American lizard, in high school. His father was an alcoholic, and he suggests addiction sometimes runs in families. He was with Jean-Michel Basquiat the night Basquiat died of a heroin overdose. He discusses euphoric recall as forgetting the bad parts of addiction and going back.

He cites Elizabeth Kolbert's The Sixth Extinction and describes the current extinction as the first man-made extinction, also called the Anthropocene. He says there are 8 billion people on Earth now, compared with 2.5 billion when he was born, and that primates and turtles or tortoises are the two vertebrate groups most threatened, with over half of each group threatened. He donated $30 million of his own money to turtle conservation, possibly more by now. The Turtle Conservancy successfully bred the plowshare tortoise, described as the rarest tortoise in the world and functionally extinct in the wild in Madagascar, for the first time in the Western world. Thirty young plowshare tortoises are being sent back to Madagascar. He worked with the species for over 20 years before the first hatchling. Leonardo DiCaprio helped with funding.

Tiger King drew 39 million viewers in its first 10 days and faced criticism, but its legacy includes the Big Cat Public Safety Act, which banned private ownership of big cats and big cat puppy mills. Goode credits its accidental origin to a snow leopard being driven in a van during reptile filming in South Florida about 12 years ago. He argues that effective advocacy casts a wide net to reach the unconverted rather than preaching only to the already converted. He identifies as an animal welfare person rather than an animal rights activist, deliberately walking a centrist line and engaging people in red states, because calling people morally repugnant shuts down dialogue.

Monsters of God shows empathy for the masculinity journey of directionless men embraced by motorcycle gangs and drug dealers, and the conclusion is that we are all complicit. It depicts skeletons in zoos' closets, including a man from West Africa exhibited in the Bronx Zoo ape house around 1915 to 1920, humans exhibited in European zoological institutions, and Native Americans in tents at Lincoln Park Zoo in Chicago in the 1950s. He received criticism from the zoo community for showing these historical abuses but argues zoos have evolved and still need to improve. Hank Molt was an intelligent reptile trader who published a list of reptiles for sale; rare species becoming endangered massively increased their value, and his paying clients were mostly zoos like San Diego and Detroit that lacked their own collectors. Hank was imprisoned after a large shipment from Southeast Asia was flagged by customs; the Endangered Species Act and CITES both took effect in 1973. After Hank went to prison, Tommy Crutchfield took over his business and became relatively rich; Hank later got revenge by putting Tommy in prison over Fiji Island iguanas. The Crutchfield-Molt feud is compared to the Joe Exotic-Carole Baskin feud.

Mario was born in Cuba; his father was a CIA operative involved in the Bay of Pigs and later used those skills for drug smuggling in South Florida. Many Miami cocaine cowboys of the '80s had been in the Bay of Pigs operation and resented JFK for the US backing out. Mario smuggled both animals and drugs; his family ran a jewelry store in Little Havana where drug dealers gathered. Janet Reno, then a Florida district attorney, targeted the drug kingpins. Mario killed an undercover informant and burned the body; he was caught and sentenced to 100 years. Before arrest, he had a compound with lions, tigers, monkeys, and reptiles, compared to Pablo Escobar's estate or Scarface, and said his addiction is animals and he sold drugs to fuel it. His release after about 12 years is treated as unexplained. He confided in the filmmaker quickly, including personal details about therapy, an affair with an employee, and motel meetings while his wife was nearby. The filmmaker describes Mario as having sadness and an unbelievable moral code, with mixed feelings about him.

Anson Wong is described as a mythical figure and the Pablo Escobar of the wildlife trade, based in Penang, Malaysia, operating for 30 to 40 years. He previously had access to major zoos and people in the United States, including Tom Schultz at the San Diego Zoo, until he was wanted for smuggling. He was eventually arrested and received one of the longest wildlife-crime sentences ever in the 1990s, reportedly seven or eight years, after the government spent millions to get him. The US government ran a five-year undercover operation; after prison he returned to Malaysia, was banned from the US, and was later arrested again in Malaysia for reptile smuggling. Fear around Wong was pervasive: Malaysian fixers avoided contacting him, and the filmmaker eventually reached him only by repeatedly calling a Malaysian number. The filmmaker deliberately delayed intervening on Tonka to pursue the larger source, framing it like drug enforcement: not just catching a small dealer, but trying to get the source.

Animal obsession and hoarding are framed as analogous to addiction, with the same pattern of filling a void, self-worth, validation, and life-ruining behavior. Coverage of animal suffering is balanced against audience tolerance: too much brutality makes viewers turn away, so the approach keeps it entertaining even amid serious subject matter. After Chimp Crazy wrapped, Tanya Hadex got another chimp in her basement and is now in prison for it. The owner of Travis tried to get another baby monkey and did get another chimp. Goode communicated with primatologists about Tonka, including Craig Stanford at USC and Russell Mittermeier. Goode says he tried to counsel Tanya Hadex after Chimp Crazy, encouraging contrition and telling her not to keep repeating the same behavior. Both hosts describe recurring using dreams about cocaine, specifically dreams involving getting cocaine out of carpet and dealing with lint. Goode says using dreams are intense and panic-inducing, but waking up brings relief.

I post highlights of long-form podcasts daily.

The recurring revenue story is clean. The operational reality is not. Uptime guarantees, field service coverage, SLA disputes, fleet maintenance costs — these eat margin fast if you haven't modeled them carefully.

Locus Robotics, Roboworx, and Aescape are putting people on a panel at RoboBusiness 2026 (Oct. 20, Santa Clara) to get into the actual mechanics: contract structure, customer success metrics, unit economics at scale.

For anyone pricing a RaaS offering right now: how are you handling the gap between promised uptime and the real cost of delivering it in the field?

transcript_30s:
ROBOTAXI
Updated 2026-09-16
Sources: Robotaxi + Owning Robotaxi Fleet bookmark folders (225 unique). Not Cybercab.

NEW TODAY
- Testers (RobotaxiRadar): Tesla hiring for driving-data collection/tracking/management in 27 cities, 15 states (NY/TX/FL/NV/CA/GA/UT/CO/MN/NC/DC/PA/LA/AZ…) — hiring signal, not Official city launch…
- Folder totals: Robotaxi 221 (+1) + Fleet 4 (0 new) → 225 unique

WHAT IT IS
- Tesla’s paid autonomous ride service. You book a car in the Robotaxi app. The car drives. There is no human driver on unsupervised rides.
- Live cars today are mostly Model Y. The purpose-built Cybercab is the volume vehicle testers say Tesla is prioritizing.
- Camera-only vision. Tesla VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy: no lidar, radar, or HD maps required for safe operation on this stack.
- This how-to merges the public Robotaxi service folder with Owning Robotaxi Fleet (owner / private-fleet economics). Not Cybercab-only bookmarks.

HOW IT WORKS
- Download the Tesla Robotaxi app and join the waitlist. Official robotaxi (Sep 2025): app is available to all; access expands over time.
- Book the ride in Tesla’s app. Elon: Tesla will not partner with Uber or Lyft. “We will have enough demand.”
- Unsupervised means no safety driver. Supervised cities still have a person in the car.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): service hours are 6am to 10pm, 7 days/week. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger. Upgraded vehicle distribution and routing so you wait less.
- Testers: you can change destination and keep the same trip for multiple stops.
- Cars return to a depot or homebase and park themselves (Houston footage).
- Ashok: FSD v15 is already running on Model Y robotaxis and will run on Cybercab.
- Testers: Tesla is limiting Model Y conversions to prioritize Cybercab, built with an unboxed modular process.
- Testers (Aug 24): Tesla expects Cybercab to replace Model Ys in the Robotaxi fleet over time and become the highest-volume vehicle there. Testers flag Sept 3 / 9/3 as the Cybercab strategy moment. Austin public Cybercab rides described as “imminent.”
- Testers (Sep 7): Cybercab expected to be actively deployed across Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet soon; Austin Cybercab wait times described as going parabolic on demand.
- Testers (Sep 7): Tesla hiring Robotaxi Fleet Support Supervisors night shift across 21 cities (Cybercabs incoming signal).
- Testers (Sep 7): Waymo Q3 2025 occupancy — 90% of trips have 2 or fewer people (two-seater Cybercab justification resurfaced).
- Testers (Sep 8): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 969 after +59 vehicles; 31 short of 1,000.
- Testers (Sep 8): Houston hub still holding ~100 Cybercabs waiting on orders plus Model Y robotaxis; little lot growth since last check — FSD v15 brain called out as the unlock.
- Testers (Sep 8): Texas Robotaxi fleet momentum — Jeff Lutz cited 432 registered autonomous vehicles incl. 45 Cybercabs; software quality cited as why Tesla can keep adding cars.
- Testers (Sep 11 TeslaZoa): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 994 after +14 vehicles; 6 short of 1,000.
- Testers (Sep 11 AIScottAdams): sleep-through long-haul thesis — lie-flat Robotaxi rides could cannibalize short- and long-haul flights (tester/AI channel, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 11 CernBasher): “Tesla Just Opened The Floodgates In Austin!” ( $TSLA video/title post).
- Testers (Sep 11 teslayoda): “Robotaxis incoming to California.” Still Testers — signal, not a new Official city launch.

- Testers (Sep 12 Alexs_jame): “BREAKING” clip framed as Elon Musk and Tesla AI celebrating a Robotaxi service launch day — tester/media claim, not Official robotaxi.
- Testers (Sep 13 gailalfaratx): Austin UT campus — Robotaxis ferrying football fans fully unsupervised (no safety supervisor); emotional “how far Tesla has come” note.
- Testers (Sep 13 niccruzpatane): Austin ride comparison — 21 Robotaxi vs 2 human Uber rides; claims Robotaxi comfort next-level (smooth turning, less heavy braking).
- Testers (Sep 13 TeslaZoa): Nashville spot — 26 Cybercabs + 7 Robotaxi validation Model Ys (33 AVs total) on public roads (signal, not a new Official city launch).
- Testers (Sep 13 herbertong / TeslaLarry): peak-demand surge capacity may matter more for profits than steady-state fleet count; Tesla need not own that surge capacity.
- Testers (Sep 13 herbertong / TeslaLarry): network efficiency (charging, cleaning, maintenance, depots, coverage) may beat raw Robotaxi count as the competitive edge.
- Testers (Sep 13 SERobinsonJr): MSM late to a 720-unit figure — tester says more are coming / already on site (fleet/Cybercab count chatter, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 14 MelvinInvests): stack thesis — Tesla owns vehicles/software/charging/customer vs Uber marketplace (tester/investor take, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 14 TeslaNewswire): Slovenia Ministry of Transport tested FSD Supervised; working toward Robotaxi approval (tester/news signal, not Official launch).
- Testers (Sep 14 RobotaxiRadar): fleet officially past 1,000 — 1,001 in service; unsupervised 305; all latest adds unsupervised (tester tracking site).
- Testers (Sep 14 TeslaZoa): Austin density — downtown Robotaxi ~every 30s; Model Y waits ~5m; visitor mix of Model Y + Cybercab rides.
- Testers (Sep 15 RobotaxiRadar): Tesla hiring for collection/tracking/management of driving data in 27 cities across 15 states (NY, TX, FL, NV, CA, GA, UT, CO, MN, NC, D.C., PA, LA, AZ listed) — hiring signal, not a new Official city launch.
HOW TO USE
- Official robotaxi: download the app, join the waitlist.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): rides run 6am to 10pm every day. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; routing upgrade is meant to cut wait time.
- Testers: booking is in the app. One Orlando rider paid with an X Money card.
- Tesla site (as quoted): app in 29 languages; service animals; space for some wheelchairs and assistive devices.
- Testers: vehicles in Nevada must be marked “Robotaxi.”
- After the Aug 20 Nevada approval, testers say Tesla still has to finish vehicle inspections, insurance, and published rates before paid rides start there.

OWNING / FLEET (from Owning Robotaxi Fleet dump)
- Elon (Feb 2026, also in Robotaxi folder): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Fleet testers frame the network like Airbnb for cars: owner adds vehicle; Tesla handles software, routing, payments, rider experience; platform fee often modeled ~25–35%; owner keeps the rest after operating costs (tester).
- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.
- Fleet / Teslaconomics: Cybercab cost chatter ~$25k–$30k; Elon told that tester production was starting in ~1 month (Mar 2026 context — treat as dated tester claim). Rough capital for a ~$1M/yr fleet ~$850k–$1M in vehicles (tester arithmetic).
- Fleet / chamath: intends to buy and deploy large fleets nationally when possible; expects payback and positive FCF in under 2 years (tester / investor claim, not Official Tesla).
- Fleet / BrianRoemmele: “all in” on buying into the owning-fleet thesis now; separate Optimus ownership program mentioned but not published in this dump.
- Fleet / tslaming (Mar 2026): then only 8 unsupervised Austin robotaxis — historical; do not use as current fleet size (Robotaxi dump Aug 23 tester: 908 total).
- Testers / Teslaconomics (Aug 25, Robotaxi folder): “owning your own Tesla Robotaxi fleet can one day make you financially free.” Still a tester slogan — no Official owner-earnings number in this dump.
- CONFLICT / caution: owner earnings, Cybercab sticker, ROI, and payback are tester models. Dump explicitly says none of it is guaranteed. Do not treat as Official Tesla guidance.

SERVICE AREA / CITIES
- Unsupervised (no safety driver), as listed May 2026: Austin, TX (launched Jun 22, 2025); Dallas, TX and Houston, TX (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Supervised (safety driver), as listed May 2026: SF Bay Area, CA (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Testers: Bay Area rides to and from SFO. Earlier: San Jose Airport pickup.
- Testers: an Orlando rider reviewed a live Robotaxi trip (Jul 2026). Aug 21 testers also list Orlando and Tampa as live; that is not on the May 2026 official city list.
- Testers (Aug 25 Teslaconomics): 7 metro areas live. Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa ramping unsupervised; Bay Area still safety-driver. Treat as tester city list, not Official May 2026 list.
- Testers (Aug 27 travel_invest): recap of Official hours post lists 6 target cities — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa. Tester translation, not a new Official city list.
- Nevada (Aug 20, 2026): full network permit for paid public service. Start small in Clark County / Las Vegas; Tesla can expand elsewhere in the state after notifying the commission.
- Testers (Aug 23): Nevada approved Tesla for up to 5,000 autonomous vehicles, up from a 10-car interim limit. Tesla said it would be “extremely happy” to have around 2,500 running within a year.
- Testers (May 2026) said Tesla was also aiming at Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa.
- Hiring and test-vehicle posts (treat as signals, not live service): Arizona, Florida, Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, California, D.C., plus Georgia/Utah/Colorado/Minnesota/North Carolina/Louisiana/Nevada (Sep 15 RobotaxiRadar: 27 cities / 15 states driving-data roles); Germany Arzfeld pilot with a safety driver and Japan Kanagawa job listings.
- Ashok: expanding to a new city is getting cheaper; the end state is operating whole states, not city by city.

ACCESS AND PLANS
- Official: Robotaxi app waitlist. Access expands as cities open.
- Testers (Aug 27 WorldlyReviewer): received an email from Tesla advertising Robotaxi. Tester report of Tesla marketing, not a new Official service announcement.
- Elon (Feb 2026): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Testers (JPMorgan via folder posts): robotaxi operating cost about $0.50–$0.60 per mile vs $2.50–$3.00 for typical ride-hail; long-term platform goal $0.30 per mile. Older Morgan Stanley note used $0.81 per mile vs Waymo $1.36–$1.43.
- Folder testers argue Tesla scales on existing Model Y / Cybercab manufacturing and Superchargers, vs lidar-heavy custom cars.
- Testers (Aug 23): Waymo’s latest self-driving hardware reportedly costs around $20K.
- See OWNING / FLEET for private-owner economics from the Owning Robotaxi Fleet folder.

SAFETY
- Elon: scale as fast as possible, but do not harm anyone. One injury becomes a worldwide headline and a regulatory clampdown.
- Ashok (Jul 2026): zero notable incidents over 380,000 unsupervised miles, across six cities in two states. Cameras only.
- Testers on NHTSA ADS data (Jun 16, 2025–Jul 15, 2026): zero collisions initiated by the Model Y ADS. Two new incidents were other drivers hitting a stopped or parked Robotaxi (Austin red-arrow stop; Dallas parked). No passengers, no injuries, no tow.
- Austin: testers said 100% of tracked robotaxi rides in that NHTSA window were unsupervised.
- Testers: 7x safer than the average human driver is an FSD claim in this folder, not a Robotaxi-only official stat.

FLEET AND INFRASTRUCTURE
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; upgraded intelligence in vehicle distribution and routing. Testers (tslaming) say that gain is backend ops (demand forecasting, fleet placement), not a self-driving software change.
- Testers (Aug 23): 908 robotaxis in the total fleet (dated). Newer tester tracking-site counts: 969 (Sep 8), 994 (Sep 11 TeslaZoa) — still Testers, not Official.

TORONTO — New evidence reviewed by The Bureau reveals that the Jiangsu Commerce Council of Canada—the Chinese Communist Party-linked business group at the center of a controversial meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney during his leadership campaign—was among the key attendees of a lavish Lunar New Year gala in January 2019, attended by senior Liberal Party organizers and hosted by Wei Wei, a United Front affiliate and Chinese organized crime target, at one of Wei’s Toronto-area mansions.

A year later, another of Wei’s residences would become the focus of a high-level York Regional Police and CSIS investigation into underground casinos, weapons stockpiles, and transnational money laundering that police allege abetted international drug trafficking.

Evidence suggests Wei Wei’s properties were used for political donations to the Don Valley North Liberal Association, a campaign in Markham–Thornhill, and a Liberal nomination contestant in the Markham–Unionville riding.

Elections Canada records show that both Wei Wei and the JCCC’s former president donated to Bang-Gu Jiang’s nomination effort in Markham–Unionville during Justin Trudeau’s tenure as Liberal leader.

The revelation deepens the controversy surrounding JCCC’s political access and linkages to figures investigated by Canadian police. During his campaign to become Prime Minister, Mark Carney denied meeting with JCCC leaders with links to Beijing’s United Front Work Department, after The Globe and Mail reported on the meeting.

The JCCC’s website was subsequently pulled offline. However, The Bureau published photographic and documentary evidence showing Carney did in fact attend a JCCC-sponsored event in Toronto—a high-level Chinese New Year reception involving key figures in the Liberal fundraising ecosystem. Among them were JCCC executives linked to a United Front PPE operation involving the same Markham riding boss photographed with Wei Wei at the January 2019 gathering at Wei’s lavish residence.

This Liberal Party official—listed as a director alongside Wei Wei of the Canada Hefei Friendship Association, which nominally hosted the January 2019 gala at Wei’s Toronto mansion—has long held fundraising and organizing roles for Liberal candidates across the Greater Toronto Area.

The newly surfaced 2019 gala—hosted on January 5, months ahead of the federal election—was held at one of Wei Wei's upscale Toronto-area homes and attended by over 40 community association leaders, business executives, and political operatives. While separate from his notorious 5 DeCourcy Court property, which was raided in a sweeping police operation, the interior photos confirm a similarly extravagant setting: crystal chandeliers, silk table settings, a decadent bar populated by dozens of wine and high-end Chinese liquor bottles, and banners for the Hefei Friendship Association (HFA).

Photographic and documentary evidence obtained by The Bureau confirms that among the attendees were Wei Wei, casually dressed and seated beneath red velvet lounge décor; the president of the Canada Hefei Friendship Association, who opened the gala with a speech promoting political and economic exchange with Anhui Province; Bang-Gu Jiang, a Liberal nomination contender in Don Valley North; and the Liberal riding boss tied to the JCCC, who played a central role in the party’s regional fundraising apparatus.

The gala also brought together leaders from the Confederation of Toronto Chinese Canadian Organizations (CTCCO), a group founded in 1985 and described in The Globe and Mail as linked to Peter Yuen, Carney’s chosen candidate to replace MP Paul Chiang in Markham–Unionville. According to The Globe, CTCCO is led by an individual who “has close ties to the Chinese consulate and attended sessions of the Chinese People’s Congress and Chinese People’s Consultative Conference, a top advisory body to President Xi Jinping.” That individual, along with the CTCCO, was debanked by TD Bank, which cited internal documents showing the organization’s transactions were flagged as involving “individuals or entity(ies) identified by media, law enforcement and/or intelligence agencies as being linked to criminal activities,” The Globe reported.
