title: Somewhere right now, an animal is dying quietly and nobody is filming it.
hook_spoken: Somewhere right now, an animal is dying quietly and nobody is filming it.
transcript_30s:
Somewhere right now, an animal is dying quietly and nobody is filming it.

No caption. No music. No one scrolling past at 2am who happens to care enough to stop their thumb for three seconds. Just silence, and then nothing.

That's the part nobody wants to talk about.

We post the rescues. We post the recoveries. We post the moment the eyes open again and the tail moves for the first time in days. What we don't post — what almost nobody ever sees — is the version of this story that doesn't have an ending like that. The version where the thumb doesn't stop. Where the street stays empty. Where "someone will probably help" turns out to be nobody at all.

I've watched thousands of rescue videos over the years. Most of them blur together. A handful of them don't. A handful of them sit in your chest for the rest of the day, uninvited, and you catch yourself thinking about them at random moments — in a meeting, in traffic, right before you fall asleep. This is one of those.

I'm not going to tell you what happens in it. That's the whole point. The second I start narrating it to you, I take something away from you that you're supposed to feel in real time, frame by frame, with your own eyes, without me softening it or spoiling it or telling you how to feel about it in advance. You deserve to watch it the way it was meant to be watched — cold, unprepared, no summary, no spoilers, no "basically what happens is."

So instead let me tell you why it matters. Why 90 seconds of footage like this can do more than a thousand articles about animal welfare statistics ever will. Why your attention — yes, your attention, the thing algorithms are fighting over every single second of your waking life — is actually one of the most valuable things you have to give right now, and you can give it for free, right here, in the next two minutes.

Here's a number that should bother you more than it probably does: an estimated 600 million dogs live on the planet right now, and roughly 80% of them are strays — unowned, unclaimed, invisible to most systems built to protect them. Cats aren't much better off. In most countries, there is no census, no registry, no 911 for an animal in trouble. There is only whoever happens to be nearby, and whether that person decides to look up from their phone.

That's it. That's the entire safety net for hundreds of millions of living creatures on this earth. A stranger. A coincidence. A person who wasn't planning on becoming anyone's savior that day but became one anyway because they refused to keep walking.

Think about how fragile that is. Think about how many animals never get that stranger. Never get that coincidence. Think about how many stories like the one in this video simply never happened, not because the animal wasn't worth saving, but because nobody was there, or nobody stopped, or nobody knew what to do, or nobody cared enough to find out.

Now think about the ones that did get that stranger.

That's what you're about to watch.

I want to talk for a second about the psychology of why videos like this hit us the way they do, because I think understanding it actually makes the experience more powerful, not less. There's a reason your chest tightens before you even know what's going to happen. There's a reason your hand instinctively wants to reach toward the screen. It's not manipulation. It's not manufactured sentiment. It's something much older and much more honest than that.

Humans evolved to respond to vulnerability. A creature that cannot speak for itself, that cannot explain what hurts or ask for what it needs, that is completely and totally dependent on the mercy of whoever is standing nearby — that triggers something in us that bypasses logic entirely. It's the same wiring that makes a crying infant impossible to ignore. It's not a choice. It's not a preference. It's biology doing exactly what it was built to do: forcing us to pay attention to the most helpless thing in the room.

Animals in crisis activate that same wiring. And when you watch one go from complete helplessness to something else — to safety, to relief, to a version of life that seemed impossible thirty seconds earlier — your nervous system doesn't process that as "content." It processes it as relief. Real, physical relief. The kind you feel in your shoulders. The kind that makes you exhale without realizing you'd been holding your breath.

That's not something I'm telling you to hype up a video. That's something I'm telling you because it's true, and because most people scrolling through their feed today are starving for exactly that feeling and don't even know it. We spend so much of our day consuming things engineered to create outrage, anxiety, comparison, dissatisfaction. Content that leaves you a little worse than it found you, even if you can't quite articulate why. This is the opposite of that. This is 90 seconds that leaves you better than it found you. That is rare. That is worth protecting your attention for.

Let me tell you something else, and this one's a little harder to swallow.

Most people who see an animal in distress do not stop. This isn't a criticism — it's just documented, repeated, boring human behavior, the same phenomenon that shows up in every study on bystander behavior ever conducted. The more people around, the less likely any individual person is to act, because everyone assumes someone else will. It's called diffusion of responsibility, and it applies just as much to a suffering animal on a sidewalk as it does to a person in trouble. Everyone sees it. Almost no one acts on it. Everyone assumes someone else already has it handled.

Which means the people who do stop — who kneel down on dirty concrete, who get their hands filthy, who lose an afternoon or a night or a week of sleep to something that isn't their problem and never asked to be — those people are not ordinary. They are functioning as a kind of exception to an extremely well-documented rule of human psychology. They are doing something statistically rare every single time they do it.

That's who made this video possible. Not a camera crew. Not a production budget. A person, or a handful of people, who looked at a situation everyone else would have walked past and decided, for reasons that probably had nothing to do with logic, that they weren't going to be the version of themselves that kept walking.

I think about that a lot. I think about how many of the best things that happen in this world happen because exactly one person refused to look away when it would have been so much easier to.

You're about to watch what that decision actually looks like, played out in real time, with no script and no safety net and no guarantee of a happy ending until the very last second confirms it. That uncertainty is part of why it works. You're not watching a story that's already been resolved and packaged and explained to you. You're watching something closer to a live wire — something that could have gone a dozen different ways, and only went the way it did because of what a handful of people chose to do while the cameras happened to be rolling.

There's a specific kind of tension that builds in videos like this, and if you've watched enough of them you start to recognize the shape of it even before you understand exactly what's happening. It's the tension of watching something helpless exist in a world that has, up to that point, given it absolutely no reason to trust anyone. Every second before the turn — before whatever moment things start to change — carries an unspoken question that you can't quite put into words but that your whole body is asking anyway: is this going to be one of the times it works out, or one of the times it doesn't?

That question is the entire engine of this kind of story. It's why you can't look away even when part of you wants to. It's why, afterward, your hands might actually be a little tense, your jaw a little tight, without you consciously deciding to hold them that way. Your body was watching just as closely as your eyes were.

And then there's the other half of the story — the half that comes after the turn, when everything that felt uncertain starts, slowly, to feel like it might actually be okay. This is the part people replay. Not because it's dramatic, but because it's the opposite of dramatic. It's quiet. It's small. It's the kind of moment that, if you weren't paying attention, you might miss entirely — and that's exactly why it hits so hard when you don't miss it. Relief doesn't announce itself with fireworks. It arrives quietly, almost shyly, like it's not sure it's allowed to be there yet.

I've seen comment sections under videos like this fill up with the same phrases over and over: "I wasn't ready for that." "Why am I crying at my desk." "Sending this to everyone I know." "This is why the internet is worth it sometimes." Those aren't marketing lines. Nobody tells people to write those. They write them because something actually happened to them while they watched, something they weren't expecting to feel on an otherwise ordinary scroll through their phone.

That's the thing about content like this — the good kind, the real kind, not the manufactured tearjerker stuff that's obviously trying to squeeze a reaction out of you. You can usually tell the difference within the first few seconds. Manufactured content feels like it's performing emotion at you. Real footage feels like it's simply refusing to look away from something true. This is the second kind. Nothing here is staged for your benefit. Nobody knew you'd be watching when any of it happened. It exists exactly as it happened, unfiltered, because someone thought it mattered enough to be seen — not by an algorithm, but by other people who might need a reminder that the world still produces moments like this.

And we do need that reminder. More than we probably admit.

If you spend enough time online, it's easy to start believing that cruelty and indifference are the default setting of the world, and that kindness is the rare exception that occasionally interrupts it. I understand why that belief forms. The algorithms that decide what you see are optimized for outrage, not warmth, because outrage keeps you scrolling longer. You are shown humanity's worst behavior far more often than its best, not because the worst behavior is more common, but because it's more profitable to show you.

Videos like this one are a quiet correction to that distortion. They're proof — not an argument, not a statistic, actual video proof — that somewhere out there, right now, someone is still willing to get their hands dirty for a creature that can't thank them in any language you'd understand. That kind of proof matters more than people give it credit for. It recalibrates something. It reminds you that the world you're being shown by your feed and the world that actually exists are not always the same world, and that the gap between them is sometimes exactly where the good stuff is hiding.

I'll say this too, because I think it's true and I don't think enough people say it: watching this kind of footage is not passive. It's not just entertainment, even though it's presented in a format that looks like entertainment. Every time a video like this gets watched, shared, commented on, it changes what gets made next. It tells whoever's out there doing this work — quietly, without much recognition, often at real personal cost — that people are paying attention. That it matters. That someone, somewhere, saw what they did and it meant something to them too.

That's not nothing. In a landscape absolutely flooded with content nobody needed, that's actually something.

So here's what I'd ask of you, and I'm not going to dress it up as anything more complicated than it is: watch it. Watch the whole thing, start to finish, without skipping ahead, without reading a summary first, without letting anyone — including me — tell you what you're supposed to feel about it before you've felt it yourself. Let it build the way it's built to build. Let the uncertainty sit for as long as it needs to sit. And when it turns — because these stories do turn, that's the whole reason they get told — let yourself actually feel that turn instead of already reaching for the next thing on your feed.

You will not regret the ninety seconds. I can promise you that much. What I can't promise is that you'll come out the other side unaffected, because in my experience, almost nobody does.

There's an old idea, repeated so often it's practically become a cliché, that you can't save every animal, every creature, every life that needs saving — and that's true, and it's also, in a strange way, exactly why the ones you can save matter as much as they do. Nobody who did what you're about to see did it because they thought they were solving the entire crisis of animal suffering on this planet. They did it because one specific, particular, individual life was in front of them, and they had the ability to change what happened to it, and they used that ability instead of walking past it.

That's the whole philosophy, really. Not "save the world." Just: don't be the person who could have helped and didn't. One creature, one moment, one decision at a time. That's how every rescue story you've ever seen actually started — not with a mission statement, but with somebody simply refusing to keep walking.

I think that's worth remembering, especially on days when the scale of everything wrong with the world feels too big to do anything about. You can't fix all of it. Almost nobody can. But you can watch this, and let it remind you that individual acts of stubborn, inconvenient compassion are still happening every single day, in places you'll never see, done by people whose names you'll never know, for creatures who will never be able to say thank you in any way you'd recognize — and that this, somehow, is still enough to matter. Still enough to count. Still enough to be worth ninety seconds of your undivided attention on a random day when you had absolutely no plans to feel anything at all.

Go watch it. Then watch it again, because the second time you'll notice details you missed the first time, when you were too busy holding your breath to notice anything except whether it was going to be okay.

And when you're done — and I mean actually done, not "I watched the first ten seconds and got the gist" done — do the one thing that costs you nothing and might matter more than you think: share it. Not because sharing it makes you a good person. Sharing a video doesn't make anyone a good person, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Share it because somewhere in your feed, right now, there is someone who needs exactly this reminder today. Someone having a genuinely terrible week who needs ninety seconds of proof that things can still turn out okay. Someone who forgot, somewhere along the way, that the world is still capable of producing moments like this one, made by people who had every reason to keep walking and didn't.

That's it. That's the whole ask. Watch it. Feel whatever you're going to feel about it, because you will feel something, I promise you that. And if it moves you the way it moved me, pass it along to somebody who could use it today.

Some days the algorithm gives you outrage. Some days it gives you comparison, or anxiety, or fifteen seconds of someone else's vacation designed to make you feel like yours isn't good enough. And every once in a while — not often, but often enough to matter — it gives you something like this instead. Something that costs you nothing and gives you back more than you expected. Something that, for ninety seconds, makes the entire absurd, chaotic, occasionally overwhelming experience of scrolling through your phone feel like it was actually worth it.

This is one of those times.

Watch it before you scroll past. You'll know within the first few seconds why I'm telling you not to skip this one.

Let me back up for a second, because I want to talk about something that doesn't get talked about enough — the people who actually do this work when nobody's watching, long before any of it becomes a video anyone sees.

There is an entire invisible economy of care that runs quietly underneath everyday life, in almost every city and every village on earth, made up of people nobody elected, nobody trained in any formal sense, nobody is paying a salary. They carry food in their car "just in case." They know which alley, which lot, which stretch of road tends to have animals in trouble, the way a lifeguard learns where the riptides are. They've ruined more shirts, more car seats, more nights of sleep than they'd ever admit to, for creatures that will never know their names.

Nobody trains for this job because it isn't a job. There's no certification. No uniform. No guaranteed outcome. Just a decision, made over and over, day after day, to keep showing up for something that offers absolutely nothing back except the fact that it needed you and you came anyway.

I bring this up because I think it's easy to watch a video like this and assume it's a one-off. A lucky break. A single dramatic moment that happened to get caught on camera. It isn't. It's one visible frame out of an enormous, ongoing, mostly unseen pattern of people choosing — repeatedly, exhaustingly, without applause — to be the exception to the rule that most of us live by, which is: not my problem, not my responsibility, someone else will handle it.

Someone else, it turns out, rarely does. Which is exactly why the someone who actually shows up matters as much as they do.

I want to say something that might sound strange coming from someone whose entire job is understanding what makes content spread, what makes people stop scrolling, what makes a hook land in the first half-second. The truth is, the best content I've ever seen didn't need any of the tricks. It didn't need a clever opening line or a pattern interrupt or a carefully engineered curiosity gap. It just needed to be true, and to matter, and to be shown to people who were capable of recognizing that it mattered.

That's rarer than you'd think. Most of what gets engineered to go viral is engineered because the underlying thing isn't actually strong enough to carry itself. You have to dress it up. You have to manufacture urgency it doesn't naturally have. This is the opposite situation. This didn't need to be engineered into something worth watching. It already was. My only job here is to make sure you don't scroll past it by accident, the way you scroll past a hundred other things today without a second thought.

Here's something I think about constantly in this line of work: attention is the only truly finite resource any of us have. Not money — you can make more money. Not time, exactly, because you don't get to choose how much of that you have anyway. Attention. The actual, present-moment capacity to notice something and let it matter to you. You get a limited supply of that every single day, and the entire modern internet is built, almost aggressively, to extract as much of it as possible for things that give you nothing back.

Every single day, your attention gets pulled toward things that were engineered specifically to be pulled toward — outrage bait, comparison bait, manufactured drama between people you'll never meet about problems that don't exist. By the end of most days, people report feeling drained, irritated, vaguely worse than when they started scrolling, without being able to point to any one thing that caused it. It's death by a thousand cuts, each cut too small to notice on its own.

This is different. This is the rare case where giving your attention to something actually gives you something back. Not content that extracts from you — content that restores something. There's a reason people say they feel lighter after watching rescue footage like this, even when what led up to the rescue was genuinely hard to watch. The relief at the end isn't just relief for the animal. It's relief for you too. Proof that things can still turn out okay is a kind of nourishment most of us are quietly starving for and don't even realize it.

transcript_30s:
Targeted Killing, Assassination and Transnational Repression: Separating State Practice from Strategic Narrative -  The available official record does not support a defensible narrative in which Russia uniquely employs extraterritorial lethal operations while other major powers merely respond to an exceptional Russian practice, but neither does it support the reverse proposition that the United States, China, Britain, France, Germany and Russia participate in an interchangeable system of politically motivated assassination; instead, the documentary record shows several legally and operationally distinct categories that are frequently collapsed into the same media vocabulary.

The United States possesses the most extensively documented public policy architecture among the states examined for deliberate lethal counterterrorism operations against individually identified or otherwise targetable persons abroad, including operations outside conventional battlefields, although no reliable official global database permits the conclusion that it is numerically the world’s largest practitioner across every category of targeted killing. In 2016 alone, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence reported 53 U.S. counterterrorism strikes outside areas then designated as active hostilities, assessing 431–441 combatant deaths and one non-combatant death, while explicitly acknowledging the inherent limitations of casualty assessment. Summary of 2016 Information Regarding United States Counterterrorism Strikes Outside Areas of Active Hostilities — ODNI

Washington has also publicly acknowledged particular individual killings, most conspicuously the 2 January 2020 killing of IRGC-Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani in Iraq, which the Department of Defense described as a defensive action ordered by the President; the legality of that operation was subsequently disputed in the United Nations human-rights system, illustrating why the fact that a state publicly invokes self-defence does not itself settle the international-law question. Statement by the Department of Defense — 2 January 2020

Russia presents a materially different evidentiary pattern because European judgments, inquiries and current U.S. criminal proceedings concern alleged or established covert killings, poisoning operations and murder-for-hire activity inside states with which Russia was not in an acknowledged armed conflict, including the legally established 2019 Berlin Tiergarten killing, the British Litvinenko inquiry’s finding of probable FSB direction, the British government’s attribution of the Salisbury operation to GRU officers, and the newly unsealed September 2026 U.S. indictment alleging an intelligence-linked network engaged in murder-for-hire and preparations for targeted killings.

China is unquestionably documented in U.S. and European institutional records as conducting transnational repression, surveillance, coercion, intimidation and attempted forced repatriation abroad, but the official material examined for this assessment does not justify placing Beijing immediately behind Washington in a quantitative ranking of extraterritorial targeted killings; doing so would transform evidence of repression into evidence of homicide without the necessary documentary bridge.

The United Kingdom and France have acknowledged lethal operations against terrorist targets abroad and therefore cannot analytically be treated as states that categorically reject targeted lethal force, whereas Germany’s official record examined here is principally that of a host state confronting foreign targeted killing, and no comparable public evidence was identified establishing a German governmental assassination programme abroad; the same caution applies to Italy, for which no equivalent official record establishing a national programme of extraterritorial targeted killings was found during this review.

The principal analytical conclusion is therefore not that “everyone assassinates,” nor that Russian extraterritorial violence is sui generis, but that major powers operate across a spectrum running from acknowledged battlefield targeting and asserted self-defence, through secret counterterrorism operations, to clandestine state-directed murder, coercive rendition and transnational repression, and that these activities engage different bodies of law, different evidentiary standards and different degrees of state accountability.

Targeted Killing and the Politics of Selective Outrage
The argument over targeted killing is being distorted less by the absence of evidence than by the refusal to distinguish different kinds of evidence. On 15 September 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice charged five alleged members of a Russian intelligence network with financing terrorism, murder-for-hire activity and preparations for targeted killings in the United States and Europe. Those accusations matter, but they remain allegations. The wider record is more uncomfortable: the United States, United Kingdom and France have themselves acknowledged deliberate lethal operations against identified individuals abroad, while European courts have attributed clandestine killings to Russian state actors and U.S. courts have convicted or prosecuted individuals linked to Iranian, Chinese and Indian state activity. The relevant divide is therefore not between states that kill and states that do not, but between legal authority, operational method, evidentiary status and political accountability.

An indictment is not a judgment, and an intelligence assessment is not a conviction
The 15 September 2026 Russian case illustrates the first discipline required of governments and serious media alike. The Department of Justice alleges that five defendants associated with Russian intelligence services financed surveillance, murder-for-hire and attacks against infrastructure in countries supporting Ukraine, yet all remain defendants rather than convicted perpetrators. By contrast, the 2019 Tiergarten murder in Berlin crossed a different evidentiary threshold when the Kammergericht concluded in December 2021, after a 14-month trial, that Vadim K. had killed Tornike K. on behalf of Russian state authorities; the judgment became final on 27 December 2021.

The Alexander Litvinenko case moved still further into judicial attribution when the European Court of Human Rights ruled in Carter v. Russia, delivered on 21 September 2021 and final on 28 February 2022, that Russia was responsible under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights. British investigators had examined more than 60 locations and sent more than 40 mutual-legal-assistance requests to 15 states. Salisbury, by contrast, remains in a different evidentiary category: in September 2018 the British government identified the suspects as GRU officers and assessed that the operation was almost certainly approved at a senior level of the Russian state, but no British criminal trial of those officers followed.

These distinctions are not legalistic decoration. They determine whether a reader is looking at a prosecutorial allegation, an intelligence conclusion, an executive attribution or an adjudicated fact. Collapsing them into a single headline category converts uncertainty into certainty and obscures the cases where attribution has actually survived judicial scrutiny.

Washington’s record is visible because Washington chose to institutionalise lethal reach
The United States is unusual among the states examined because its use of targeted lethal force has been repeatedly acknowledged by the government itself. In calendar year 2016, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence reported 53 counterterrorism strikes outside areas then designated as active hostilities, assessing 431–441 combatant deaths and one non-combatant death. Those figures were not a complete register of every operation, but they documented a standing capability rather than an exceptional improvisation.

That architecture remained visible in individual operations. On 31 July 2022, two Hellfire missiles killed al-Qaida leader Ayman al-Zawahiri in Kabul at 06:18 local time, according to the Department of Defense, nearly one year after the withdrawal of conventional U.S. forces from Afghanistan. In October 2019, U.S. special operations forces raided the compound of Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi in Syria; U.S. Central Command reported that 11 children were removed from danger, two men were detained and five Islamic State members presenting a threat were killed before Baghdadi detonated a suicide device.

The same system also produced documented failure. On 29 August 2021, a U.S. drone strike in Kabul killed 10 civilians, including up to seven children, after intelligence had incorrectly identified the vehicle and its occupants as an imminent ISIS-K threat. U.S. Central Command later acknowledged error, confirmation bias and intelligence failure. In calendar year 2024, the Department of Defense assessed that U.S. military operations had killed two civilians and injured two others under its reporting methodology. The lesson is not that transparency resolves the legality of every strike, but that the U.S. record is unusually measurable because policy, operations and failures have all generated official documentation.

Britain and France sit inside the same operational universe, but with thinner public ledgers
On 21 August 2015, an RAF remotely piloted aircraft killed British national Reyaad Khan near Raqqa. Prime Minister David Cameron subsequently told Parliament that the National Security Council had considered Khan a direct threat, that the Attorney General had advised on the legal basis and that the Defence Secretary had authorised what Cameron explicitly called a “targeted strike”. The Intelligence and Security Committee later stated that there was “no doubt” Khan posed a very serious threat to the United Kingdom, while declining to substitute itself for a court on the legal question.

Britain’s current operational role remains visible. Operation SHADER recorded four publicly listed RAF strike dates in Iraq and Syria during 2025, while on 3 January 2026 British Typhoons and a Voyager tanker joined French aircraft in striking a Daesh underground facility north of Palmyra with Paveway IV precision-guided bombs. The United Kingdom therefore cannot be described as a state standing outside targeted lethal operations; the defensible distinction lies in the legal basis claimed, the theatre, the target and the degree of disclosure.

France presents a comparable but institutionally different pattern. Operation CHAMMAL currently deploys about 600 French military personnel in the Levant, while French Rafales flew between 18 and 21 sorties per week in several reporting periods during May and June 2026. Earlier Barkhane operations targeted senior jihadist leadership directly: Abdelmalek Droukdel, emir of al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb, was killed on 3 June 2020, while Adnan Abu Walid al-Sahraoui, leader of Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, was killed in an August 2021 operation involving armed drones and Mirage 2000D aircraft.

The comparative problem is therefore not whether Britain and France possess the capacity to identify and kill individuals abroad; official records show that they do. The problem is that neither publishes a comprehensive historical ledger comparable to the partial American record, making any numerical hierarchy between Washington, London and Paris methodologically unsound.

China’s documented coercion is extensive, but the lethal comparison is weaker than the rhetoric
China belongs in the record, but not where a simplistic ranking would place it. U.S. federal proceedings have established a substantial body of evidence concerning Chinese transnational repression, including surveillance, stalking, intelligence collection and coercive repatriation. In April 2025, former New York police officer Michael McMahon was sentenced to 18 months in prison and an $11,000 fine for conduct linked to Operation Fox Hunt; another defendant, Quanzhong An, received 20 months and approximately $5 million in financial penalties, including about $1.3 million in restitution, after pleading guilty to acting as an illegal PRC agent in a coercive repatriation campaign.

The intelligence dimension is equally concrete. Shujun Wang was convicted on all four counts in August 2024 after prosecutors established that he cultivated Chinese democracy activists while secretly reporting to Ministry of State Security officials. Tang Yuanjun separately pleaded guilty after acknowledging that between 2018 and June 2023 he passed names, photographs, recordings and other information concerning U.S.-based democracy activists to the MSS.

What those cases establish is systematic extraterritorial repression; what they do not establish is a public evidentiary basis for describing China as the world’s second-largest practitioner of overseas targeted killing. The distinction matters because surveillance, coercive return, attempted intimidation and assassination belong to the same continuum of state repression but are not interchangeable operational events.

Europe is no longer merely observing these methods; it has become operational terrain
Europe’s exposure is measurable because the continent is simultaneously projecting military power and protecting the infrastructure, communities and institutions that foreign states increasingly target. As of July 2026, the European Union reported 22 ongoing Common Security and Defence Policy missions and operations, involving more than 3,500 military personnel and 1,300 civilian personnel. By early 2026, more than 87,000 Ukrainian personnel had been trained under the EU Military Assistance Mission, while Operation ASPIDES had protected more than 2,390 merchant vessels and provided close protection to more than 720 ships in the Red Sea.

Italy illustrates the overlap between external commitments and internal exposure. Operation Prima Parthica maintains about 300 personnel in the land component and 400 in the air component, with Italian forces having trained approximately 50,000 Iraqi and Kurdish personnel. In June 2025, however, the Interior Ministry reported that more than 29,000 sensitive sites were under protection inside Italy, including more than 10,000 critical infrastructures and roughly 1,000 sites connected to American or Israeli interests. External policy is therefore transmitting directly into domestic security expenditure and policing requirements.

Germany’s position is even more structurally sensitive because the Bundeswehr’s August 2026 mandate ceilings included 500 personnel for Counter-Daesh and Capacity Building Iraq, 550 for NATO Sea Guardian, 350 for ASPIDES, 300 for IRINI, 300 for UNIFIL and 400 for KFOR, while the 2025 Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution report identified Russia, China and Iran as the principal foreign intelligence threats and highlighted espionage, sabotage, transnational repression and cyber operations.

France has moved the same problem into counter-intelligence doctrine. On 6 January 2025, the Direction générale de la sécurité intérieure formally defined transnational repression as foreign-government activity intended to identify, locate, monitor, intimidate, forcibly repatriate or attack political opponents abroad. The definition matters because it places the surveillance of dissidents and potential lethal action inside the same national-security continuum rather than treating them as unrelated crimes.

Britain shows what happens when foreign-state coercion becomes a domestic security metric
The United Kingdom currently provides the clearest publicly quantified example of the internalisation of state threat. In March 2025, the Security Minister told Parliament that the number of MI5 state-threat investigations had increased by 48 per cent in one year and that Britain had responded since 2022 to 20 Iran-backed plots presenting potentially lethal threats to British citizens or residents. MI5 subsequently stated in its 2025 threat update that it had tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots in the latest one-year reporting period.

The legal response followed the operational assessment. The National Security Act 2023 created modern offences concerning espionage, sabotage and foreign interference, while the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme, in force from 1 July 2025, imposed registration requirements on activity directed by foreign powers and created an enhanced tier initially focused on Russia and Iran. By May 2026, the Home Office was publicly defining transnational repression to include surveillance, stalking, coerced return, assassination and attempted assassination.

This development is more consequential than any single foiled plot because it signals the fusion of counterterrorism, counter-espionage and organised-crime methods. MI5 and Germany’s BfV have both warned that Russia and Iran increasingly use criminal or low-level proxies for surveillance, arson, sabotage and potentially violent tasks, allowing sponsoring states to lower cost, obscure attribution and exploit the lag between intelligence suspicion and judicial proof.

The next 12–24 months will be decided by attribution, not rhetoric
The European institutions have already shifted. In November 2025, the European Parliament adopted a resolution on transnational repression by 512 votes to 76, with 52 abstentions, stating that roughly 80 per cent of recorded cases were attributable to ten states including China, Russia and Iran. In June 2026, Parliament adopted a further resolution by 434 votes to 128, with 104 abstentions, calling for a common EU definition, stronger information sharing, law-enforcement training and an EU-level response architecture.

The cost of inaction over the next 12–24 months will therefore fall less on diplomatic communiqués than on intelligence services, police forces, ports, rail networks, energy operators, defence companies and diaspora communities. Italy is already protecting more than 29,000 sensitive sites; Britain is already recording double-digit potentially lethal foreign-state plots; Germany is already treating espionage, sabotage, cyber activity and transnational repression as one threat environment; France has already moved the issue into its counter-espionage doctrine.

The decisive contest will be over attribution speed. If European governments cannot connect criminal proxies, financial transfers, cyber reconnaissance and intelligence tasking quickly enough to establish state responsibility, adversaries will continue to exploit the space between suspicion and proof. If they can, the political argument will become harder to manipulate: not because targeted killing disappears from Western state practice, but because legal military action, covert murder, transnational repression and prosecutorial allegation will finally be judged on evidence rather than affiliation. - debuglies.com/2026/09/16/tar… via @https://debuglies.com

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a Rs 10 lakh penalty on ride-hailing platform Rapido for alleged misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices, unfair contract terms and the use of deceptive “dark patterns”, the government said on Tuesday.

The action against Roppen Transportation Services Pvt Ltd, which operates Rapido, follows a sector-wide examination of cab and bike-taxi aggregators over practices including pre-ride tipping and dynamic pricing.

The CCPA said Rapido prompted riders to pay more while their bookings were still being processed. Messages displayed on the app included, “Higher the price, higher the chance of getting a ride” and suggestions to add Rs 10, Rs 20 or Rs 30 when drivers were not accepting the quoted fare.

According to the regulator, the app first quoted a fare and, after the booking was made, prompted users to increase the amount, creating an impression that paying more was necessary to secure the ride.

The CCPA classified the practice as “confirm shaming”, a dark pattern that creates urgency or fear of losing a service unless the consumer agrees to an additional payment.

The authority also flagged the colour-coded “Set your price” slider, saying it could influence users’ pricing decisions.
The CCPA noted that tips are ordinarily voluntary and should not be presented as a condition for receiving a service. It said Rapido’s submissions on tips were rejected.

The authority has also issued notices to Uber, Ola, Rapido and Namma Yatri under the 2023 dark-pattern guidelines. Its examination of Uber and Ola is ongoing. #rapido #TheAssamTribune @rapidoapp_

transcript_30s: There is a GitHub repo that shows the exact instructions Claude and ChatGPT follow before you type a word. System Prompts Leaks is a folder tree of the system prompts behind the big AI chatbots, one folder per company: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, Meta, Microsoft, DeepSeek, Mistral, Kimi, Qwen, Cursor, Notion, Perplexity and more. You open the folder for the AI you use, click the file, and read the rules in plain markdown. The Claude Fable 5.1 file alone is 7,810 lines and the ChatGPT 5.6 file is 1,845 lines. Two lines that got me: Claude is told to never use bullet points when declining a task, because the extra care softens the blow. ChatGPT is told to never share the font files in its container, especially when you ask directly. Coverage as of Sep 14 includes Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Claude Code, ChatGPT 5.6, Codex GPT-6-Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Grok 4.6, Kimi K2.6 and DeepSeek. The Washington Post built an interactive story on it and CEPS built a live dashboard from the files. 66,602 GitHub stars as of Sep 14, CC0. The catch: the README says captured verbatim and does not say how, so treat the long versions as community-verified until a vendor signs off. It is a reading collection, nothing to install.

transcript_30s:
We've started converting 2-3x more lead magnet commenters by using this AI agent that watches, scores, and messages your warmest leads automatically as they engage:

A comment on your lead magnet tells you three things:

- The person has the problem
- They trust you enough to engage publicly
- They want what you're offering

If a founder at a 20-person B2B agency comments "AGENCY" on your lead magnet about booking more inbound calls, they wrote half your opening DM for you.

Here's how I'd build the agent with Claude Code:

Step 1 is the watch list

Set up Apify to scrape every comment on every lead magnet post you publish, the moment it goes live.

Pull commenter profile URLs, job titles, company names, and comment timestamps into a central Airtable or Google Sheet automatically.

Dedupe on the commenter profile URL so the same person never triggers twice on the same post.

Step 2 is ICP scoring

Have Claude read every commenter's LinkedIn profile and score them 1-10 against your ICP definition.

The scoring prompt should include: job title match, company size range, industry fit, seniority level, and whether their profile description suggests they have the problem your lead magnet addresses.

Throw out anything below a 7 before you spend a single enrichment credit. Only the highest intent leads move forward.

Step 3 is enrichment

LinkedIn profile URL into Clay for company domain, headcount, revenue, and industry.

Flag everyone who scores 8+ as priority. They get the DM sequence first, same day the comment comes in.

Step 4 is the outreach

Claude writes the opening DM from the signal itself.

"Hey, saw you grabbed the [lead magnet name], are you currently dealing with [specific pain point the lead magnet addresses] or have you already found a way around it?"

Qualifying question 24 hours after resource delivery and then send a case study once they respond. Specific time and date once fit is confirmed. Five messages maximum.

Step 5 is the repeat engagement filter

This is where it gets interesting.

The agent checks every commenter's history weekly. If the same person has commented on two or more of your lead magnets in the last 30 days, they get flagged as a hot lead regardless of their ICP score.

Someone who has engaged with your content multiple times is not a cold prospect. They are someone who keeps coming back because they still have the problem and haven't solved it yet.

Those people get a separate sequence that references both engagements specifically.

"Noticed you grabbed both the [lead magnet 1] and the [lead magnet 2] over the last few weeks. Sounds like [specific problem] is still something you're working through. We've helped a few people in your exact situation fix this in [timeframe], would it make sense to spend 15 minutes seeing if we could do the same for you?"

A cron job runs the full thing every morning. New comment, score, enrich, DM sequence, weekly repeat engagement check. The warmest leads in your pipeline are already raising their hand on your content. This system just makes sure none of them slip through.

transcript_30s:
when I don’t know how to design a site / app

usually not a talent problem.  
it’s a tab problem.

too many pretty screens. zero decisions.

so I stopped collecting “inspo” and started sorting it by question.

---

first: split the job

I keep mixing 3 things:

- product (what people actually tap through)
- marketing (hero, pricing, CTA, store)
- wow (3D, awards, agency scroll)

wow waits.  
flow first.

---

write the problem in one line

before figma / cursor:

> 4-step onboarding. value before signup.

can’t write that? I don’t need inspiration yet.

---

where I look

how do real apps solve this  
→ mobbin  
→ refero if it’s more web/saas  
→ page flows if I need timing, not a screenshot

is this component even a thing  
→ component.gallery same tabs / empty state / pagination across 20 systems. ego down.

ai feature, how do people understand it  
→ aiverse miniguides  
discover → instruct → observe → refine → adapt

landing / cta / pricing  
→ saaspo, land-book, cta.gallery not awwwards. awards don’t sell plans.

what should it feel like  
→ recent (old godly) or one awwwards site  
mesh3d only if the product actually needs 3D

motion  
→ jitter + 60fps / appmotion  
one transition. not a reel.

agent output looks like slop  
→ impeccable (audit / polish / typeset)  
or huashu if I need a direction, not beige + inter + nested cards

---

30 min when I’m stuck

10 — one flow on mobbin  
5 — 3 versions of the component  
5 — one microinteraction  
5 — one craft reference. one.  
5 — keep / kill list

longer than 30 = procrastination with taste.

---

what I write down

not “love this.”

- what you read first
- dense or airy
- one weird choice that works
- what I won’t copy because it isn’t our product

steal decisions. not pixels.

---

north stars

clarity: linear, things, superhuman, cash app, stripe, notion, perplexity  
ceiling: awwwards  
floor: stuff people open every day

---

if an agent is designing

don’t say “make it nice.”  
give: 1-line problem + 2–3 real refs + an audit.

inspo isn’t the prompt.  
the prompt is the brief. the gallery is evidence.

---

parking this for future-me who “just checks dribbble for a sec.”

steal it if useful.  
got a better source for real flows? send it.
